title: You Think Cats Solve Door Latches by Logic, Yet Stopwatch Curves Proved Blind Reward

acts.name: 1897 William James's Basement & Fifteen Slatted Crates at Columbia
sentences: You think clever animals solve latches using logic!
Yet a simple stopwatch shattered that cozy myth!
This is the true story of Edward Thorndike.
Here is what went wrong with pet folklore.
Before eighteen ninety-eight, scholars trusted tall tales from pet owners.
At twenty-three, Thorndike wanted stopwatch proof instead of stories.
Harvard banned his animals so William James offered his basement!
In eighteen ninety-eight, Thorndike built fifteen slatted crates at Columbia.
One fish dish sat outside — and that wasn't the strangest part.

acts.name: 160 Seconds Down to 6 Seconds & The Missing Aha Cliff
sentences: How did a hungry cat open those crate latches?
Escaping took pressing a pedal or pulling a cord.
One tough crate linked three separate latches in order.
On trial one, cats pawed for one hundred sixty seconds, like a tangled kite.
Then one lucky paw pressed the pedal by chance!
The weighted door swung open to the dish!
Did escape time drop straight down on trial two?
Over twenty-five trials, time sloped to six seconds, like a gentle ramp.
Waiting for a sudden genius flash was a total nightmare.

acts.name: Imitation Failure, Law of Effect & Reward Stamping
sentences: Could a rookie cat learn faster by watching an expert?
Rookie cats watched experts escape ten times, like a front-row seat.
Placed inside the crate they still pawed from zero!
Guiding a cat's paw by hand taught zero shortcut.
Instead of reasoning about strings, brains kept moves that won food.
Thorndike named this rule the Law of Effect!
Fast rewards fire your nucleus accumbens, your reward center, on contact.
Each win stamps that move into your basal ganglia, your habit engine.
But here's the twist: do hidden latches tell the whole story?

acts.name: 1917 Visible Insight vs 1932 Truncated Law of Effect
sentences: In nineteen seventeen, Wolfgang Kohler spotted a fair critique.
Thorndike hid his cords so no animal saw cause.
With visible tools, your prefrontal cortex, your planner, connects the steps.
Apes stacked visible crates under fruit in sudden flashes!
Did scolding erase bad habits as fast as reward?
In nineteen thirty-two, Thorndike tested thousands of human choices.
He bravely repealed half of his own famous law!
Rewards wire lasting habits while scolding fades away fast.

acts.name: Skinner Chambers & Modern AI Reinforcement Learning
sentences: How did homemade crates reshape modern computing and robots?
Skinner built conditioning chambers directly on Thorndike's curve.
In nineteen seventy, Richard Herrnstein turned reward rates into math.
Across thirty trials, learning robots run that loop, like a room thermostat.
Digital agents try moves, score wins, and prune mistakes.
Simple packing slats birthed modern artificial intelligence reinforcement learning!
The researchers were left completely stunned.
One basement crate rule scaled from cats to computers.

acts.name: Shrinking Delay to Stamp In Everyday Skills
sentences: How can you use the Law of Effect tonight?
Ten hours of bike lectures fail without pedaling, like a closed cookbook.
Your motor cortex, your movement strip, must test the move itself.
Shrink the gap between good action and clear reward!
Fast praise builds habits five times faster than scolding, like a desk bell.
Phone apps hook your thumb using tiny instant wins.
Pair small immediate wins with the craft you love.
Which proves mastery is not sudden genius, but letting fast wins stamp skill in.
